As I mentioned in #119980, we should add cases where the duration is not 1.0 seconds (default value).

I have updated the test cases to use a duration of 8 seconds instead of 1.

This is done by scaling every keyframe's time by 8.
What do you mean "Nearest" here?

It means the nearest keyframe _before_ the current time.

In this case, the nearest keyframe before t = 1.0 is at t = 0.0.

So if I understand right, it should be:
`t = M (Between the keys { t = L, v = X.f } and { t = N, v = Y.f })`

In the case of nearest interpolation, only the keyframe before the current time matters, regardless if the playback is forward or backward.

Which is to say,
* t = 1.0 -> Nearest is t = 0.0
* t = 3.0 -> Nearest is t = 0.0
* t = 5.0 -> Nearest is t = 4.0
* t = 7.0 -> Nearest is t = 4.0
* t = 9.0 -> Nearest is t = 8.0

> t = M (Between the keys { t = L, v = X.f } and { t = N, v = Y.f })

Writing it like this may mislead the reader into thinking that it's "nearest keyframe in terms of distance" and thinking that the answers should be something like this instead:
* t = 1.0 -> Nearest is t = 0.0
* t = 3.0 -> Nearest is t = 4.0
* t = 5.0 -> Nearest is t = 4.0
* t = 7.0 -> Nearest is t = 8.0
* t = 9.0 -> Nearest is t = 8.0

It's still unclear what you mean from your comment. You should have the documentation team review it and make sure the comment is clear enough for most people to understand. cc @Mickeon @AThousandShips

@TokageItLab 
I have reworked the comments to explain what `t` is as well as the behavior of nearest interpolation.

---

Side note, but none of this is documented behavior: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_animation.html#enum-animation-interpolationtype

I was only able to deduce the behavior by digging into the source code.
I think it is still not clear. It is not possible to tell from the comments why there is a comment of "Nearest" in the "Discrete" test, or what value the "XX" in "Nearest is XX" refers to.

@TokageItLab 

I have reworked the comments for the discrete test to be more explicit and verbose to the best of my abilities.
If you were to write this in a Discrete test, it would be better to describe it as "Latest passed key is" rather than "Nearest".

But it's not actually discrete. As written in the comments, the default callback mode is `ANIMATION_CALLBACK_MODE_DISCRETE_FORCE_CONTINUOUS`. It's technically "continuous" and using nearest interpolation, but processed slightly differently.

So instead of using `ANIMATION_CALLBACK_MODE_DISCRETE_FORCE_CONTINUOUS`, you should use `ANIMATION_CALLBACK_MODE_DISCRETE_RECESSIVE`, just like the `AnimationPlayer`'s default.

Testing it with `ANIMATION_CALLBACK_MODE_DISCRETE_FORCE_CONTINUOUS` doesn't make much sense. While it can test whether `FORCE_CONTINUOUS` is working, it doesn't serve as a test to verify that discrete updates are functioning properly.
`ANIMATION_CALLBACK_MODE_DISCRETE_FORCE_CONTINUOUS` is the default behavior (specifically for AnimationTree and not AnimationPlayer) and is what I'm testing here.

Ah, I just remembered that FORCE_CONTINUOUS also causes segment offsets. Since Force Continuous is exist for blending, only the update timing is set to Continuous; the direction of key acquisition follows that of Discrete. So, in the case of reverse playback, the results will differ from those of Nearest+Continuous.

However, it would be a good idea to add a test to verify that RECESSIVE matches FORCE_CONTINUOUS. That’s exactly what was fixed by #119871.

In any case, the word "Nearest" is likely to cause confusion, so we should probably use “latest” or “last passed key” instead.

As for why I'm not testing `ANIMATION_CALLBACK_MODE_DISCRETE_RECESSIVE`, I actually believe it to be *broken* here. Consider the simple backward playback case. I can imagine the last processed key for t = 7.0 and t = 5.0 to be t = 8.0 since it should be the first key processed in a backward playback, but the answer here is actually t = 0.0! When I was writing unit tests for Camera3D 2 years ago, I discovered that most of the methods straight-up don't work with the rather obscure "frustum" projection mode and it was undocumented. The solution back then was just to not test them because obviously we can't just submit broken tests. I believe this case to be the same.

Is this an issue that only occurs when using time scale? Can you reproduce the problem in the actual Editor?

If the issue can be reproduced, it is a bug, so you may skip that test. However, if it cannot be reproduced, there might be a problem with the processing of the first frame of the AnimationTree in the test scene. In general case, to playback AnimationNode uses a one-shot, StateMachine or something, and I would expect that a seek with a process time of 0.0 occurs as part of its reset behavior. The reason for this might be that it wasn't done in the test scene.

Also, as I have said many times, even if you are going to skip the recessive test, you must avoid using the word "Nearest" here.

Changed "nearest" in comments to "latest".

---

The above issue with `ANIMATION_CALLBACK_MODE_DISCRETE_RECESSIVE` can be reproduced in editor by switching between the `RESET` clip and the `anim` clip in `AnimationNodeAnimation`. (I've only checked the latest branch)

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b35d3e42-2a49-4519-a2f7-af5b62b3c370

The animation's keyframes look like this:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e22fa302-e0df-4ea3-ae7d-81049f506588

MRP: [mrp-discrete-reverse-playback.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28711140/mrp-discrete-reverse-playback.zip)

That said, I am still not confident about the behavior of `ANIMATION_CALLBACK_MODE_DISCRETE_RECESSIVE`. Not confident enough to write test cases for it. And not for a lack of trying (I've spent the last 3 hours or so on it and I'm still having a hard time explaining each "answer". I've also been unable to verify 100% parity with AnimationPlayer doing so.)

I'd like to ask that unit tests for `ANIMATION_CALLBACK_MODE_DISCRETE_RECESSIVE` be implemented in a separate pull request, by someone more knowledgeable than I am. I'm willing to admit that this is a skill issue and I'm not cut for it. (And if you'd like to reject the whole PR because of this that's also fine by me)

> start_offset should be ignored.

Since this is a regression by #119871, it must be fixed.
